Dark matter cannot be seen directly because it does not emit, absorb, or reflect light. Yet scientists know it exists because of its gravitational effects on stars, galaxies, and the structure of the universe. They observe how visible objects move, calculate how they ought to move given the matter they can see, and conclude that something invisible must be influencing their behaviour. Something similar happens in politics.

Parties, politicians, election results, and public statements are visible. But the interests, obligations, relationships, and incentives that determine political behaviour are often concealed. Political dark matter becomes apparent when decisions begin to defy the explanations offered for them.

South Africans should become more sophisticated in detecting these invisible forces. Much political scrutiny concerns whether parties are genuine organisations or vehicles established to advance hidden interests. These are important questions, but they are only the beginning. A party may be entirely real, enjoy genuine electoral support, and have legitimate political ambitions while remaining subject to powerful influences never disclosed to its supporters. The more important question is therefore often not whether a political party is real, but whether its decisions are truly its own.

The aftermath of South Africa’s 2026 local government elections provides an especially useful setting in which to apply this test. The African National Congress (ANC) suffered a severe electoral setback, falling to its lowest share of the vote in its history, with more hung councils in the country than ever before. And coalition negotiations in many municipalities are still ongoing, with continuing uncertainty over who may be the mayors in some of South Africa’s major cities.

To the public, parties claim that coalitions will be agreed on with an eye on stability, service delivery, accountability, and respecting electoral outcomes. Yet voters should apply a more demanding test. Why would a party reject an arrangement that appears to advance its stated objectives? Why might a politician insist that one partnership is politically impossible, only to embrace another involving greater ideological contradictions? Why would parties that campaigned bitterly against one another suddenly discover an overriding common purpose? Why would a political organisation accept an arrangement that weakens its electoral prospects or strengthens forces it previously condemned?

There may be rational answers. Coalition politics requires compromise. And politics makes strange bedfellows, as the old adage goes.

But when the explanation offered does not adequately account for the decision made, voters should begin looking for the gravitational effects of interests absent from the official account.

Those interests may involve access to government procurement resources, protection of patronage networks, municipal appointments, political financing, personal rivalries, business relationships, or private commitments to influential individuals. They may also involve ideological loyalties or political debts accumulated over decades. There may even be elements of a South African “deep state” that are attempting to influence the direction of political parties and coalition arrangements. A decision that appears irrational when measured against public promises may become entirely rational once an undisclosed interest enters the calculation.

South Africans should therefore pay particular attention to decisions that repeatedly benefit the same interests despite changes in electoral outcomes. If a party loses support but retains influence over public resources, if politicians survive failures that would ordinarily destroy their careers, or if supposedly incompatible organisations repeatedly cooperate when particular offices are at stake, the pattern deserves examination. Just as astronomers infer dark matter from the movements of visible objects, political observers can identify possible hidden interests by tracing otherwise inexplicable outcomes.

Coalition government makes this particularly important. Where no party wins a majority, the power to determine who governs shifts towards negotiations between party leaderships. Smaller parties can acquire disproportionate influence, while larger parties may be excluded. This is a legitimate feature of democratic coalition formation, but it also creates opportunities for interests never presented to voters to influence government formation and the allocation of public resources.

The answer is more rigorous scrutiny. Voters and journalists should compare decisions against parties’ principles, electoral incentives, and previous behaviour. They should ask who benefits, who sacrifices, which relationships remain constant, and whether the public explanation accounts for the observable facts.

Above all, they should ask whether a political decision would still make sense if the only interests involved were those publicly acknowledged by the politicians responsible for it.

That is the lesson of political dark matter. What cannot be seen directly may nevertheless be detected through its effects. When political decisions make no sense, when explanations do not ring true, and when inexplicable outcomes repeatedly favour the same interests, voters should sharpen their scrutiny.

The most important question in South African politics may increasingly not simply be who holds power, but what invisible interests are pulling those who hold it.
